facts.claim: "How to be Me (OurVinyl Sessions)" is track 1 on the four-track release "Colton Bowlin | OurVinyl Sessions", credited to Colton Bowlin and OurVinyl, released 18 November 2025. Its running time is 3:41.
The release is copyrighted 2025 OurVinyl TV, Inc. and distributed by Stem. The other tracks are "Time for Sale", "Josey Wales" and "Something I Wrote Today".
A country discography blog lists the OurVinyl session versions as recorded at OurVinyl Studio in Nashville, TN.

The original studio version of "How to Be Me" was recorded in Athens, GA, with David Barbe as producer. It appeared on the three-song EP How to Be Me, with "Take the Time" and "Turn the Page", released 10 October 2025.
The How to Be Me EP is on State Line Records, marketed and distributed by Thirty Tigers, and "Turn the Page" on it is credited to producer David Barbe.
Bowlin said the EP's songs came from a time when he was trying to work out who he is, who he isn't and who he wants to be. He said it is about not having all the answers all the time.
Holler described the EP as a stripped-down collection about a young man trying to find his way back to himself. It deals with the pieces of a breakup and the weight of regret.
In a Q&A just before the EP's release, Bowlin named "Turn the Page" and the title track "How to Be Me" as the songs he was most looking forward to from the EP.
Bowlin was born and raised in Albany, Kentucky, on the Kentucky–Tennessee line. His 2024 debut album was Songs from the Holler, which included "Josey Wales", and his 2026 follow-up is Grandpa's Mill.
Bowlin grew up working in his grandfather's feed mill. He says the old-timers' tall tales there inspired many of the stories in his songs.

draft:
The guitar does two jobs at once on **How to be Me**. Colton Bowlin fingerpicks a rolling arpeggio while his thumb keeps a bass line walking underneath, so the song carries its own floor and its own motion with nothing else in the room to help. The tempo sits in the middle, unhurried. The voice comes in slightly raspy and mid-range, pitched like someone talking across a kitchen table rather than projecting to the back of a hall. There are no harmonies, no second voice to soften a line or tell you it'll be fine. It's one person and one instrument, and that turns out to be the right size for what the song is about.

Bowlin has said the songs on the How to Be Me EP came from a stretch when he was trying to sort out who he is, who he isn't, and who he wants to be, and that the record is about not having all the answers all the time. Holler called the EP a stripped-down set about a young man trying to find his way back to himself, picking through the pieces of a breakup and the weight of regret. Put that next to the title and the feeling comes clear. This isn't a song of arrival. It's the in-between state where you've lost the version of yourself you knew and haven't built the next one yet. The plain delivery fits that. There's no grand vocal move to claim a confidence he's admitted he doesn't have.

This session version, the opener of a four-song OurVinyl set cut in Nashville, strips the song further than its first life. The original was produced by David Barbe in Athens, Georgia, for the three-song EP on State Line Records, and Bowlin named it, along with "Turn the Page," as the one he was most eager for people to hear. Here the production is dry and close, with a natural room around it and no polish, so the rasp and the pick noise are right there. The relaxed groove keeps the regret from curdling into self-pity. It moves along like a man walking while he thinks.

Bowlin grew up in Albany, Kentucky, on the Tennessee line, working his grandfather's feed mill and soaking up the old-timers' tall tales that later fed his songs. That puts him squarely in the Appalachian strain of country and Americana, and the comparisons to Tyler Childers and Sturgill Simpson make sense. The difference is that this song trades the porch-yarn storytelling of that tradition for something more private: no characters, no tall tale, just a young man taking his own measure. The set also revisits "Josey Wales" from his 2024 debut, Songs from the Holler, so the session holds both sides of him at once.

The song sticks because it gives you permission to not be finished, and lets you sit with someone who's honest enough to say so out loud.
